query: Which method can be used for reduce the sintering temperature, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using 3D ink‐extrusion printing to form the green part prior to sintering enables a reduction in the required sintering temperature because the process produces a highly porous structure with enhanced particle contact.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory alloy powders mixed with a binder to form a printable ink.
generation.intervention: Fabricate a green part by 3D ink‐extrusion printing at room temperature and then sinter at lower temperatures than conventionally required.
generation.conditions: Controlled binder removal and sintering conditions in atmospheric or inert environments similar to those used for conventional sintering.
generation.structural_mediator: Porous microstructure with a high specific surface area that reduces diffusion distances between particles.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced contact among particles in the 3D printed green part lowers the activation energy required for densification during sintering, thereby reducing the necessary sintering temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Comparable densification and final mechanical properties can be achieved at a lower sintering temperature relative to conventionally pressed powders.
generation.baseline: Conventionally prepared powder compacts that require higher sintering temperatures for full densification.
generation.boundary: The magnitude of temperature reduction may depend on powder composition, binder type, green density, and the efficiency of binder burnout.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect is supported by the formation of a porous green structure in 3D ink‐extrusion methods, the exact reduction in sintering temperature and its universality for all refractory alloy systems remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using the same refractory alloy powder: one set via conventional pressing and one set via 3D ink‐extrusion printing followed by binder removal. Sinter both sets under identical conditions while gradually decreasing sintering temperatures for the printed samples. Track densification and mechanical properties as functions of sintering temperature.
measurements: Dilatometry to assess the onset and degree of densification
Porosity evaluation via microscopy or mercury intrusion porosimetry
Mechanical property determination (e.g., hardness, yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 3D printed samples do not achieve similar densification or mechanical properties at significantly lower sintering temperatures compared to conventionally pressed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD.
